SeriesLinearAlgAccessor API Reference¶

Back to Series API Reference

This page is the landing page for the linear-algebra workflow entered through Series::linearalg and continued through SeriesLinearAlgAccessor. The accessor groups operations whose shapes are governed by vector, matrix, and batched-matrix rules rather than ordinary elementwise broadcasting.

Using This Reference¶

  • Use the method rail to open one accessor method at a time.

  • Each method page owns its signatures, shape contract, gradient model, verified examples, failures, and previous/next navigation.

  • Start at Series::linearalg when you need the accessor calling model; start here when you already know which operation you need.

Read This First¶

The accessor supports two equivalent call styles:

auto out1 = left.linearalg.matmul(right);
auto out2 = left.linearalg(right).matmul();

The first style passes the right operand to the method. The second binds it when the accessor proxy is created and then calls a zero-argument method. Use the first style in ordinary code unless binding a peer makes a longer chain easier to read.

Several operations also have a direct root spelling such as left.matmul(right). The accessor spelling is useful when you want the code to announce that an operation follows linear-algebra shape rules.

Method Pages¶

Norms¶

  • norm: global Euclidean or Frobenius magnitude

Factorizations¶

  • cholesky: triangular factorization of symmetric positive-definite matrices

  • qr_q and qr_r: orthonormal-basis and triangular factors of a rectangular matrix

  • svd: obtain singular vectors and singular values together

  • svd_u, svd_s, and svd_vh: request one SVD component

Determinants And Inversion¶

  • det: signed scale factor of each square matrix

  • inverse: multiplicative inverse of each nonsingular square matrix

  • logdet: real logarithm of each positive determinant

  • slogdet: determinant sign and logarithmic magnitude in one result

Products¶

  • matmul: rank-polymorphic vector, matrix, and batched matrix multiplication

  • mm: matrix-matrix multiplication with a strict two-dimensional contract

  • mv: matrix-vector multiplication

  • dot: non-conjugating inner product of two vectors

  • vdot: vector inner product that conjugates the left operand

Matrix Transformations¶

  • matrix_power: compose a square transformation an integer number of times

  • matrix_exp: convert a linear rate into a finite transformation through the matrix exponential

  • pinverse: SVD-defined pseudoinverse for square, rectangular, and rank-deficient matrices

Linear Solves¶

  • triangular_solve: forward or backward substitution through a triangular coefficient matrix

  • cholesky_solve: solve an SPD system from a reusable Cholesky factor

  • cholesky_inverse: construct an SPD inverse from a Cholesky factor

  • lu_solve: solve a general nonsingular square system

The handwritten reference now covers the complete SeriesLinearAlgAccessor surface.

Choosing A Product¶

Use matmul() when the code intentionally accepts more than one rank pattern: vectors contract, matrices multiply, and leading batch dimensions broadcast. Use mm() or mv() when rank is part of the contract and an accidental vector or matrix should be rejected. Use dot() for two one-dimensional vectors. Use vdot() instead of dot() when the left input may be complex and the Hermitian inner product is intended.

Choosing A Determinant Operation¶

Use det() when the signed determinant itself is the required value. Use logdet() when the determinant is known to be positive and the algorithm works in the real logarithmic domain. Use slogdet() when sign must be retained or the magnitude may span a large numeric range. Use inverse() when the inverse matrix itself is needed; singular matrices have a zero determinant and no inverse.

Choosing A Matrix Transformation¶

Use matrix_power() for an integer number of repeated applications, including zero and negative powers. Use matrix_exp() when a matrix represents a continuous linear rate whose finite transformation is required. Use pinverse() when a rectangular or rank-deficient map needs a least-squares reversal rather than a strict square inverse.
